progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From p03: "water in q, fuel in n"; Δm = initial − final; ΔHc = −q ÷ n per mole of fuel; results about half the data values; heat to the can, clamp and air makes q too small; evaporation makes n too big; capping the burner and reweighing at once. From skills-s07: word, feature, fix (name the feature of the method and its effect before proposing a fix); G02 applies the same habit to an anomalous trial for the first time. From c07: the data values (−726, −1367, −2021 kJ mol⁻¹); ΔHc is per mole of fuel; kJ per gram is a different quantity. From m6-c03: q = mcΔT with c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹; keep the digits, round at the end. From Year 11: n = m ÷ M; molar masses from the data sheet; significant figures (decimal places in a subtraction).
progression.startsWith: An unseen methanol dataset. The video opens: A combustion question hands you three numbers that look alike: the water's mass, its temperature rise, and the mass of fuel burnt.
progression.stopsAfter: calculating ΔHc from raw spirit-burner data; the percentage of released heat that reached the water; the mass of fuel needed when only a stated fraction reaches the water; calculating a trial's ΔHc, identifying it as anomalous by its cause and excluding it from the mean; checking each answer's size, unit and sign.

teaching.task: A combustion question gives you a water mass, a temperature rise and a fuel mass that all look alike. How do you give each its job, get the molar enthalpy and the share of heat that reached the water, run the calculation backwards, and decide whether an odd result belongs?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why the water's mass goes in q: the water is what warms (2b). Why the fuel's mass lost gives n: ΔHc is per mole of fuel (2b, 2e). Why ΔH is negative: heat is released (2c). Why only about half reaches the water: the rest warms the can and the air (2d). Why the heat released is bigger than q(water): only 45% reaches the water (3b). Why multiplying by 0.450 must be wrong: heat lost means more fuel, so the answer must exceed the no-loss mass (3d). Why trial 3 is anomalous: same heat, more mass lost, so that fuel never heated the water (most likely it left without burning), making n too big (4c). Why it may be excluded: its cause is identified (4c, 4d). Why averaging it in is wrong: an explained faulty trial drags the mean away from every good trial (4e).
teaching.conversationalApproach: A combustion question hands you three numbers that look alike (the water's mass, its temperature rise and the mass of fuel burnt), and each has one job, so every walkthrough sorts the givens before calculating: the water goes into q, the fuel's mass lost gives n, and delta H is minus q over n. Q1 (methanol from raw data) finds q, n and the molar enthalpy one line at a time, then compares the heat released by complete combustion with the heat the water gained to give the share that reached it; Q2 runs backwards from the heat a planned warming needs, divides by the share that reaches the water, and turns heat into moles and moles into a mass of ethanol; Q3 asks whether one of four propan-1-ol trials is anomalous, works trial 3 the same way, finds the cause (extra mass lost for the same rise) before dropping it, and averages the trials that fit. Each question ends with its spoken, crossed classic mistake (dividing by grams, multiplying by the share instead of dividing, averaging all four trials), and the decision board gives the steps for any combustion calculation.
teaching.openingDecision: A combustion question hands you three numbers that look alike: the water's mass, its temperature rise, and the mass of fuel burnt. Each one has a single job. The water's mass and its rise go into q. The fuel's mass gives n. Swap them, and the answer can be out by a factor of a hundred or more. Here are three HSC-style questions, and the last one hides a result that doesn't belong. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it, one step at a time.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a): every mass, temperature, c, M and data value; Q2's 45.0% and its "same apparatus" condition; Q3's table, the shield and lid, "fresh water", M and c. Nothing answer-bearing during the holds; the check strip dims.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p55), as printed: "conduct a practical investigation to measure and reliably compare the enthalpy of combustion for a range of alcohols" Related Year 11 content (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 4, recalled, quoted from the official 2017 syllabus DOCX): "investigate enthalpy changes in reactions using calorimetry and q = mcΔT (heat capacity formula) to calculate, analyse and compare experimental results with reliable secondary-sourced data, and to explain any differences". Practice and transfer only: the coverage rows stay with chem-m7-p03 (conduct and errors) and chem-m7-c07 (equations and data values); G02 adds practice rows, not first coverage. starts at the route's "Separate water mass, temperature rise and fuel mass" and stops at its "Calculate molar enthalpy and evaluate an anomalous result". Three questions, each a chain of steps with one trap: (1) methanol from raw burner data: ΔT, q from the water, n from the burner's mass lost, ΔHc, then the percentage of the released heat that reached the water (trap: dividing by grams); (2) the reverse: the mass of ethanol needed for a planned temperature rise when only a stated fraction of the heat reaches the water (trap: multiplying by the fraction instead of dividing); (3) a results table for propan-1-ol with one anomalous trial: calculate it, judge it by its cause, and take a suitable mean (trap: averaging all four). Not here: the method, set-up, errors list and improvements (chem-m7-p03); answer technique for validity, reliability and accuracy (skills-s07); balancing combustion equations and energy per gram (chem-m7-c07); graphing a homologous series (left out; see near-match check); the calorimeter's heat capacity; percentage uncertainty; bond enthalpies.

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in the G01 and G03 layout: top-left the question card (stem, data, table and demands, as an exam prints them, with the tag "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience"), kept readable through each question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Raw data: q, n, ΔH", "Backwards: heat to mass", "Table: is it anomalous?"), hidden during each attempt because it names the method. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used. A check strip on the far left carries four rows, "water in q?", "fuel in n?", "kJ, per mole, sign?", "makes sense?", and ticks the row each scene uses; it dims to an outline during every countdown. Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Working follows the C03 and p03 staging: equation strip, one stage per line, earlier lines dimming, one kept chip into the next scene. Colour key from p03: water quantities (m, ΔT, q) orange, fuel quantities (Δm, n) blue, ΔH teal; amber only for underlined givens. Clutter rule (owner): besides the question strip and the check strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each tag fades when the next cue lands.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on and the job sorter drops three grey number chips into a water tray and a fuel tray; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes with its spirit burner plate or trial table kept readable; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given in amber as it is used while q, n and delta H write one stage per line in their colours, earlier lines dimming to kept chips; the heat split bar fills its share of the energy released; a number line places three fuel masses for the backwards question; the trial strip draws a dashed band and rings trial 3's mass; each classic mistake writes as a chip and takes a red scribble cross; the check strip returns full size as the two-column decision board, row by row; scene crossfade with settle.
